reconcile.connective: Harmonizers read the texts by audience — God's anger toward His own people is brief, while His anger toward the unpardoned endures for ever.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells' Skeptic's Annotated Bible lines up the verses to show Scripture saying God's anger lasts a moment, not forever, forty years, and forever — irreconcilable as stated.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999), contra/anger.html

excerpts.author: Matthew Henry
excerpts.attribution: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14)
excerpts.excerpt_text: Though God may for a time lay his own people under the tokens of his displeasure, yet he will not retain his anger for ever, but though he cause grief he will have compassion; he is not implacable; yet against those that are not of the remnant of his heritage, that are unpardoned, he will keep his anger for ever.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: States both poles explicitly and harmonizes them: anger is not retained for ever toward His own people, yet is kept for ever against the unpardoned.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14), on Micah 7:18
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry harmonizes the brevity and permanence texts directly by distinguishing God's temporary anger toward His own people from His enduring anger toward the unpardoned.
